Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

lost internal rotation · films of both hips · stable vs unstable · atypical: look for an endocrine or renal cause · keep off it and pin in situDoes a child of 8 to 15 with a limp and hip-to-knee pain have films of both hips, and can the child walk even with crutches?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Age 8 to 15 limp hip, groin, thigh or knee pain films of both hips; cross-table lateral if the slip is unstable (cannot walk even with crutches); lost internal rotation supports it
  • Suspected slip off the leg now (crutches or a wheelchair) urgent in situ screw fixation; never force it back
  • Under 8 or over 15, underweight or short consider an endocrine or renal cause
What it is

Femoral epiphysis slips back and down off the neck, through the growth plate (physis)

Most common hip disorder of adolescence, usually at 8 to 15 years; average age 12 in girls, 13.5 in boys

Driver

Probably a weakened physis shear force, greater with obesity the slip

Triggers

Obesity: 63% weigh at or above the 90th percentile, but it is not required

Growth spurt: tall, thin adolescents slip too non-modifiable

Male sex non-modifiable

Genetic factors non-modifiable

Endocrine abnormalities (hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment, hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism); renal disease

Chain

Physis, proposed: weak plate shear epiphysis slips through the hypertrophic zone

Exam: limp; lost internal rotation; hip turns outward on passive flexion

Vessels: kinked, or pressed by a hematoma osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) often early osteoarthritis

Insights

Knee pain can come from the hip: the obturator nerve usually carries it

Walking sets the risk: a child who cannot walk even with crutches has an unstable slip, with more complications

Course, stage by stagedetail behind the chain
FirstMay begin as stiffness that eases with rest, then a limp, then pain down the front and inner thigh to the knee
PainPoorly localized: hip, groin, thigh, buttock, low back or knee; worse with squatting, long sitting, cyclingThe hip may be missed until the slip worsens
LaterPainful hip motion with limited flexion, abduction and internal rotation; limp or Trendelenburg gait; leg turned outAn early exam may not show it
TypeAbout 90% are stable; by duration, acute under 3 weeks, chronic 3 weeks or more, acute-on-chronic a flare of a chronic slipAbout 88% of unstable slips had earlier symptoms
UntreatedUsually progresses; osteonecrosis and collapse of the epiphysis can follow if the blood supply fails
2Urgent risks
SlipA suspected slip, at any stage
Usually progresses

If a slip is suspected, choose no weight bearing until it is ruled out or fixed, plus urgent orthopedic referral.

UnstableCannot walk, even with crutches

If the slip is unstable, choose urgent fixation, never a forceful reduction.

FeverFebrile and toxic, hip held flexed and turned out

If fever or toxicity comes with the hip pain, choose a Kocher criteria count, then urgent ultrasound-guided aspiration if septic arthritis is suspected.

AbuseThe story is vague or does not fit the age or the injury

If the history does not fit, choose an evaluation for inflicted injury, with child and caregivers interviewed apart.

3Differential
Look-alikes in school age and adolescence, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Slipped capital femoral epiphysisLimp, vague hip to knee pain, lost internal rotation8 to 15; symptoms over weeks; turns outward on passive flexion; epiphysis below the Klein line
Adductor strain (groin pull)Groin painFollows an injury or activity; lost internal rotation points to the hip instead
Limp and vague hip pain over weeks to months; lost internal rotationAbout 4 to 10; femoral head flattened or fragmented rather than displaced
Limp, sometimes after a viral illnessUnder 10; a course of weeks argues against it
Febrile, toxic, hip held flexed and turned outAny age; Kocher criteria: fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) over 40 mm/h, white cell count over 12,000/µL
Femoral neck stress fractureRunner whose training just went up; groin painAdolescent athlete; hurts to hop; films normal, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) shows it
Avulsion fracture of an anterior iliac spineHip pain, age 12 to 25Sudden, after a forceful movement; seen on the film
Knee pain in an adolescentAdolescent; the tibial tubercle is tender
Limp, groin pain, limited abductionFilm shows a chronically dislocated hip, not a slipped epiphysis
Limp with painNight pain
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Knee pain; knee exam and knee films normalHip disease felt in the kneeExamine the hip; films of both hips
Weeks of groin pain, then a minor fall and now unable to walkAcute-on-chronic unstable slip; a femoral neck fracture needs high-energy traumaOff the leg; urgent fixation
A cold last week, but 13 years old with 3 weeks of painNot transient synovitisFilms of both hips
Short, underweight, or under 8 or over 15Possibly an endocrine or renal causeThyroid, growth hormone and kidney tests as well as fixation

Pause point. The bait: groin pain called a muscle strain and sent to physical therapy, or a stiff hip offered bracing or a spica cast. Lost internal rotation with a widened, irregular physis is a slip before the head visibly moves, and only fixation stops it; strain is rare at this age, and bracing and casting treat infant dysplasia.

5Diagnostic criteria
Confirm by film Views – AP (anteroposterior) and frog-leg lateral of both hips · Unstable – AP of both hips and a cross-table lateral of the slipped side · Klein line – drawn along the top of the femoral neck, it normally crosses the epiphysis; in a slip the epiphysis sits below it · Physis – wider than the other side: a slip even before the head moves · Films normal – MRI or ultrasound helps when a slip is still suspected

Why order itSCFE is bilateral in about one-fifth of patients; 18 to 50% across series.

6Severity
Stability, by weight bearing
TypeRecognize itIt means
StableWalks, with or without crutches; about 90% of slipsOsteonecrosis under 10%
UnstableCannot walk, even with crutchesOsteonecrosis in as many as 20 to 50%

Also gradedOn the frog-leg film the head is displaced under one-third of the neck width (mild), one-third to one-half (moderate) or over one-half (severe).

7Treatment
1

Nowslip suspected or seen

No weight bearing (crutches or a wheelchair) and urgent orthopedic referral

The aim is to stop the slip and prevent osteonecrosis, chondrolysis and impingement.

2

Surgeryas soon as it is diagnosed

In situ fixation with a single screw across the physis

Never force the head back: forceful reduction can cause osteonecrosis.

3

Complicationnew pain or stiffness after fixation

Image the hip for osteonecrosis or chondrolysis

Chondrolysis is sudden cartilage loss, most often from a pin that entered the joint unseen, so the joint space narrows; osteonecrosis shows first as sclerosis and lucency, then collapse of the head.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Stable slipSingle screw in situBracing, casting, traction and physical therapy do not stop a slip
Unstable slipUrgent fixation, usually in situTiming of surgery and the value and manner of reduction are debated; never a forceful reduction
Atypical patientFixation plus an endocrine and renal workupHypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment, hypogonadism
Other hip painlessFilms now; consider pinning only if risk is high Who gets itYounger patients, obesity, an endocrine disorder, or follow-up unlikely.Prophylactic pinning of the healthy hip is not recommended for most patients
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
After fixationGraded return over about 6 months; after a stable slip, running and contact sport may resume once the growth plate closes
The next 18 monthsWatch the other hip: when it slips, it is often within 18 months
Years laterEarly osteoarthritis can follow osteonecrosis, or impingement after a severe slip heals out of position
Practice
  1. 14-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain tripped on a stair this morning; now cannot bear weight at all, even with crutches left leg lies externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: left femoral epiphysis displaced posteriorly → Unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis → unable to bear weight even with crutches defines an unstable slip: osteonecrosis risk up to about half; keep him off it and pin urgently, without reduction
  2. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed today with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis below the 5th percentile for height and the 10th for weight growth slowed over the past 2 years Fatigue and constipation HR 62/min · BP 100/64 mm Hg → Screen for hypothyroidism, a growth hormone disorder, panhypopituitarism and renal osteodystrophy → short and underweight is atypical at any age: look for an endocrine or renal cause alongside fixation
  3. 12-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis today pinning is scheduled right hip: no pain, full internal rotation Body mass index above the 95th percentile Afebrile · radiographs were taken of the left hip only → Radiographs of the right hip now → both hips are imaged at diagnosis: about one-fifth of patients have bilateral slips (18 to 50% across series)
  4. 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of aching right knee pain and a limp knee: no effusion, no tenderness, full painless motion ligament tests normal Plays football; no specific injury Afebrile · knee radiographs normal → Examine the hip → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip: a slip refers pain to the knee through the obturator nerve
  5. 14-year-old girl 5 months after screw fixation of a slipped left capital femoral epiphysis new left groin pain and stiffness hip motion now limited in all directions Afebrile · radiograph: narrowed joint space; femoral head round, without sclerosis; screw position unchanged → Chondrolysis → a narrowed joint space means lost cartilage, and a stiff, painful hip with that film after fixation is chondrolysis, most often from a pin that entered the joint unseen; osteonecrosis shows first as sclerosis and lucency, then collapse of the head; an unchanged screw argues against hardware failure
  6. 16-year-old girl, a cross-country runner, with 3 weeks of right groin pain worse with each run; now hurts to hop on the right leg recently doubled her weekly mileage Afebrile · radiographs of both hips normal → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping with normal films after a training increase: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for a femoral neck stress fracture
  7. 12-year-old girl with 3 weeks of right thigh pain since a minor fall today she cannot bear weight on the right leg right leg held externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: right femoral epiphysis displaced off the neck → Forceful closed reduction of the slip → forcing the epiphysis back raises the risk of osteonecrosis: keep her off the leg and pin it where it lies
How NBME framed it: question 1

Previously healthy 13-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain and a limp no fever; not in acute distress height 50th percentile, weight 97th, body mass index above the 97th left hip: internal rotation and abduction limited; internal and external rotation to 75 degrees hurt; externally rotates on passive flexion Right hip and both knees normal T 37 °C · pulse 90/min · RR 20/min · BP 116/75 mm Hg AP and cross-table lateral films: irregular widening of the left femoral physis; mild osteopenia of the left femoral head and neck

Analgesia and weight-loss counseling given; next step?

Competing answers
  • Physical therapy: weeks of pain and stiffness; but it treats a strain after an injury, and there was none.
  • Abduction bracing: limited abduction; but it treats DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) in infants.
  • Traction: a painful hip and a limp; but it pulls a fractured bone to length; there was no trauma.
  • Spica cast immobilization: holding the hip still; but it holds an infant hip reduced for DDH.

Down to two: internal fixation or spica cast immobilization. Internal fixation: groin pain, lost internal rotation and a widened, irregular physis are a slip even before the epiphysis visibly moves; every other option treats another hip problem.

Pairs with The Limping Child: age and time for every limp. Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: the Kocher count and aspiration for a febrile, painful hip.
Transferable rule

A stereotype is a prior, not a rule: when the exam fits and the patient does not, trust the exam and ask why.
